headline: Marine Parkway Bridge After Dark: Bass Working the Shadow Lines on the Last Ebb
subhead: Bay bass have gone nocturnal and structure-bound — fluke and weakfish are picking up the daytime slack in the channels.
body_markdown:
I launched the kayak off Aviation Road at Floyd Bennett Field before six on Thursday, mostly because I wanted to beat the heat and the boat traffic, and partly because that ramp puts you right into the mouth of the bay without fighting a current the whole way out. Paddled the edge toward the Marine Parkway Bridge and let the last of the incoming push me along the channel drop-off. That's the play in August — pick your access point to match the tide, not the other way around. Kayak in the morning while it's calm and cool, truck to the bridge or the surf at night when the real bite happens.

Because right now, the bass have checked out of the shallow bay during the day. Water up top is sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s across most of the flats, and stripers don't want any part of that with the sun up. They've slid out to the cooler structure — the bridge pilings, the deep channel bends, the inlet edges — and they're only really feeding hard at dawn, dusk, and full dark. We flagged this exact shift last week, said to fish the last hour of the ebb into dark and the first couple hours of the new outgoing after midnight, and that's precisely what's been producing. I fished the bridge Tuesday night on the tail of the ebb, eeling live snakes under a fish-finder rig, 2-ounce egg sinker, right down in the current seam off the pilings on the Rockaway side. Two fish to 30 inches, one right at the slot line that went back, both on that last hour before the tide went dead slack. Guys drifting bucktails — bone white, 1-ounce — through the same seam on the change back to outgoing picked up a couple more just after midnight.

During the day, though, it's fluke and weakfish carrying the bay. This is peak fluke season and the bay's holding up its end — channel edges off Cross Bay Bridge, the deeper holes inside Grassy Bay, and the flats off Canarsie Pier have all been giving up keepers. Nothing gigantic, mostly 17 to 20 inches, but steady if you work the drift right. Half-and-half white/chartreuse Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the outgoing, has been the most consistent combo. Bring some Berkley Gulp Swimming Mullet in pink shad too — a few of the better fish this week came on that when the plain white wasn't drawing strikes.

Weakfish have been mixed in with the fluke on those same channel edges, especially early morning before the boat traffic picks up. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but a few keeper-class fish in the 16 to 18 inch range came off the bottom near the Marine Parkway Bridge rip on bucktails tipped with squid strips, fished right on the bottom during the last two hours of the outgoing. If you're marking bait balls on the sounder near the bridge, slow down and jig it — that's where they're holding.

Canarsie Pier this week has been snapper central. If you've got a kid or you just want steady light-tackle action without driving out to the ocean beaches, small silver spoons or tiny bucktails under a bobber off the pier are producing non-stop juvenile bluefish in the afternoon. It's not glamorous but it's fun, and it's free — no permit needed there, unlike most of the NPS lots right now which are sold out for the season.

Surf side, Fort Tilden and Breezy Point are still the after-dark bass program if you've got your Fishing Access Pass. The 193rd Street lot and 222nd Street lot both require it around the clock this time of year, so don't roll up without one. I fished the groins off 193rd Street Tuesday on the outgoing — same story as the bridge, quiet until the last hour of the ebb, then a couple bass in the mid-20s came through chasing something in the wash. Swim shads and darters worked better than bucktails there; the water's clean enough right now that a subtler presentation gets more looks.

We're heading into a neap tide around the 5th and 6th, which is going to soften the current everywhere — the bridge rip, the inlet, Grassy Bay. When that happens I'd downsize presentations across the board: lighter bucktails, slower retrieves, smaller profile eels. Weaker current means the fish don't have to commit as hard, so give them more time to find your bait.

One more thing I'm watching closely — it's early August, and this is exactly the window where the first false albacore or bonito scouts start showing at the inlet mouth if the water stays clean and the bait stays thick. Nothing confirmed yet in the bay, but I'd keep a light spinning rod rigged with small metal — Deadly Dicks, epoxy jigs — in the truck just in case something silver and fast starts busting bait off the Marine Parkway rocks. It hasn't happened yet, but the calendar's right for it.

Next week, if this stable weather holds, I'd keep splitting time the same way: fluke and weakfish on the channel edges during the day, bass at the bridge and the surf on the last of the ebb into full dark. If a front pushes through and stirs up the bay, the bite could get moodier fast — but as of now, the pattern's holding.
